content: 1. Individuals with suspected or confirmed infectious tuberculosis (TB) are advised to take measures to minimize the transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to healthcare workers and other individuals in healthcare settings. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty in the evidence of effects. 2. Initiating effective TB treatment promptly in individuals diagnosed with TB disease is strongly recommended to reduce the transmission of M. tuberculosis to healthcare workers, individuals in healthcare facilities, and others in high-risk settings. This is a strong recommendation, albeit based on very low certainty in the evidence of effects. 3. Respiratory hygiene practices, including proper cough etiquette, are strongly recommended for individuals with suspected or confirmed TB to reduce the transmission of M. tuberculosis to healthcare workers, individuals in healthcare facilities, and others in high-risk settings. This recommendation is strong but based on low certainty in the evidence of effects. 4. Environmental controls, such as upper-room germicidal ultraviolet (GUV) systems, are conditionally recommended to reduce the transmission of M. tuberculosis to healthcare workers, individuals in healthcare facilities, and others in high-risk settings. This recommendation is based on moderate certainty in the evidence of effects. 5. Ventilation systems, including natural, mixed-mode, mechanical ventilation, and recirculated air through high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters, are conditionally recommended to reduce the transmission of M. tuberculosis in high-risk settings. This recommendation is based on very low certainty in the evidence of effects. 6. The use of particulate respirators, as part of a comprehensive respiratory protection program, is conditionally recommended to reduce the transmission of M. tuberculosis to healthcare workers and others in high-risk settings. This recommendation is based on very low certainty in the evidence of effects. 7. Healthcare facilities and congregate settings pose a significant risk for acquiring TB, including multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), particularly for individuals living with HIV and healthcare workers. Evidence indicates an increased risk of TB among healthcare workers and medical/nursing students with patient contact, as well as among individuals in prisons, refugee camps, and detention centers, where overcrowding exacerbates the TB epidemic. 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on TB prevention and infection control include core components of infection prevention and control (IPC) programs and TB-specific interventions to reduce M. tuberculosis transmission at the facility level. These guidelines emphasize administrative controls, environmental controls, and respiratory protection measures. 9. Routine HIV testing services should be offered to all individuals with presumptive or diagnosed TB. This is a strong recommendation, despite low-quality evidence. Additionally, all household contacts of individuals with HIV-associated TB should be offered HIV testing services, particularly in high HIV burden settings. In low HIV burden settings, household contacts with TB symptoms may be offered HIV testing as part of their clinical evaluation. 10. HIV partner services should be offered to individuals with HIV-associated TB. This includes voluntary HIV testing for partners and contacts of HIV-positive individuals, facilitated by trained providers. Provider-assisted referral for HIV testing is an effective strategy to extend HIV testing, prevention, and treatment services to sexual partners and household members. 11. For individuals living with HIV and diagnosed with TB, antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated as soon as possible, preferably within two weeks of starting TB treatment, regardless of CD4 cell count. Exceptions include cases with signs of meningitis, where ART initiation may need to be delayed. 12. Routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is strongly recommended for all individuals living with HIV and active TB disease, regardless of CD4 cell count. This recommendation is supported by high-certainty evidence. 13. Advanced HIV disease, defined as a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease, is associated with a high risk of mortality, even after starting ART. Children under five years of age living with HIV are also considered to have advanced HIV disease. WHO recommends a package of interventions, including screening, treatment, and prophylaxis for opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and adherence support for individuals with advanced HIV disease. 14. Tuberculosis is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among individuals living with HIV. Integrated care for HIV-associated TB, addressing both TB and other comorbidities such as severe bacterial infections, cryptococcal disease, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, can significantly reduce mortality. 15. WHO encourages collaboration between TB and HIV programs to expand access to integrated care for individuals with advanced HIV disease and TB. This includes implementing evidence-based interventions, such as those demonstrated in the REMSTART and REALITY trials, which showed reduced mortality and improved outcomes with enhanced care packages. 16. Early initiation of ART for individuals with HIV-associated TB is critical for reducing morbidity, mortality, and HIV transmission. TB and HIV programs should ensure that ART is offered as early as possible, preferably within integrated services or TB facilities.
